object.dateLabel: 17 March 1907 (recording session, Victor Talking Machine Company)
object.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; aria from Leoncavallo's Pagliacci (1892)
object.description: The accomplishment here is not the aria but the record. On 17 March 1907 the Neapolitan tenor Enrico Caruso stood before a recording horn in the Victor Talking Machine Company's studio and sang 'Vesti la giubba', the clown Canio's lament from Leoncavallo's Pagliacci, in which he must put on his costume and make the audience laugh while his heart breaks. The disc is generally reckoned the first gramophone record to sell a million copies. Caruso's warm, powerful voice suited the crude acoustic process better than anyone else's, and his Victor Red Seal discs, sold at premium prices, persuaded the public that a phonograph belonged in the home. He became the first star made by recordings, earning more from records than from the stage. The photograph, from the Bain News Service, shows him listening to a Victrola. The visitor hears the 1907 recording itself, now in the public domain.
facts: Caruso made his first records in a Milan hotel room in 1902 for the Gramophone Company; he recorded 'Vesti la giubba' three times, in 1902, 1904 and 1907.
His Victor contract eventually guaranteed him $100,000 a year, and his records are said to have earned him some two million dollars over his career.
All United States sound recordings made before 1923 entered the public domain on 1 January 2022 under the Music Modernization Act.
